questions.q: A test has mean $\mu = 70$ and standard deviation $\sigma = 10$. You scored $x = 85$. What is your Z-score?
questions.explain: $Z = \frac{x - \mu}{\sigma} = \frac{85 - 70}{10} = 1.5$: you are 1.5 standard deviations above the mean. $15$ is the raw distance before dividing by $\sigma$.

questions.q: If the scores are (approximately) Normal, about what percentile does $Z = 1.5$ correspond to?
questions.explain: $\Phi(1.5) \approx 0.933$, so about 93% of a Normal population lies below $x$. This reading is only valid for (roughly) Normal data.

questions.q: What does standardizing a skewed dataset with $Z = (x - \mu)/\sigma$ do to its shape?
options: Keeps it skewed — it only shifts the center to 0 and scales the spread to 1
questions.explain: Standardization is a shift and a scale; the shape of the distribution is unchanged. Skewed data stays skewed, so bell-curve percentiles don't apply to it.

questions.q: Why does standardizing input features help gradient descent?
options: It reduces the number of features
Features on very different scales create a long, skinny loss valley where gradient descent zig-zags; standardized features give a rounder bowl
It guarantees the global minimum is zero
It makes the learning rate irrelevant
questions.explain: With features like square footage (thousands) vs. bedrooms (1–5), the loss surface is elongated. Z-scoring puts features on a level playing field and lets descent head more directly to the minimum.
